text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: NORA
text: Imagine you're a buyer at a large manufacturer. Your biggest supplier has just told you prices are going up twelve percent because of new tariffs. You have a call with their sales director on Thursday. You've done two procurement courses in your career, and you passed both. Do you feel ready?

speaker: JAMES
text: Most people wouldn't. And that's the gap today's company is trying to close. Knowing the theory of negotiation is one thing. Sitting across from someone who negotiates for a living, with your company's margin on the line, is something else.

speaker: NORA
text: Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time and look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'm James. Our series follows the companies in the portfolio of Levine Leichtman Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Beverly Hills. Today it's Skill Dynamics, a company that trains procurement, supply chain and trade compliance teams at large corporations.

speaker: NORA
text: The usual note before we start. Everything we discuss comes from public sources as of November 2026: company press releases, its own research report, trade press, and the private equity firm's pages. When something is our opinion or an inference, we'll say so. When a number comes from the company itself, or from a survey the company ran, we'll flag that too. And nothing here is investment advice.

speaker: JAMES
text: And that flag matters today, because several of the most interesting numbers come from Skill Dynamics' own research.

speaker: NORA
text: So give me the one-sentence version.

speaker: JAMES
text: Skill Dynamics sells role-based digital training, skills assessment and, since July 2026, AI coaching tools to procurement, supply chain and trade compliance teams in big companies. By its own count, it has served more than five hundred and twenty customer companies and more than three hundred and fifty thousand learners.

speaker: NORA
text: And why is it interesting right now?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because in July 2026 it launched an AI Learning Suite, with three tools called Coach, Pulse and Expert. And the way its chief executive framed that launch is the thesis of this whole episode. He said the challenge organisations describe is not a shortage of learning content.

speaker: NORA
text: Which is a striking thing for a content company to say.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a very striking thing. When general AI tools can produce explanations of almost any topic for free, a company whose business has been built on a content library has to answer a hard question. If content isn't scarce any more, what are customers actually paying for?

speaker: NORA
text: Let's find out.

speaker: NORA
text: Start with the basics. Where did it come from?

speaker: JAMES
text: The company was founded in 2011 under a different name, Procurement and Supply Chain Academies. In April 2021 it rebranded as Skill Dynamics. The old name tells you the original idea quite well. Academies, as in structured programmes for a specific profession, rather than a general course catalogue.

speaker: NORA
text: Who are the customers?

speaker: JAMES
text: Large corporates with procurement and supply chain functions. Think of the buying teams at a big manufacturer, a retailer, a pharmaceutical company or an energy business. Those teams can be hundreds of people, spread across countries, with different levels of experience. A company like Skill Dynamics sells training programmes tailored to their roles.

speaker: NORA
text: Where is it based?

speaker: JAMES
text: This is a small puzzle. The private equity firm's portfolio page lists Hasselt, in Belgium. But the company's own About page says it's headquartered in the UK, a transaction database lists Reading in England, and the company's own press releases have been datelined Reading. So our best reading is a UK headquarters with a Belgian connection, but we can't fully resolve it. The company also says its team is spread across the United States, Europe, the Middle East and China.

speaker: NORA
text: Who runs it?

speaker: JAMES
text: The chief executive is Sam Pemberton, who took over in March 2022. His predecessor, David Rajakovich, had led the company for about twelve years, according to the announcement of the change. The leadership team listed on the company's site includes Davina Quarterman as chief revenue officer, Richard Jones as chief technology officer, and a handful of others covering HR and legal, marketing, professional services and engineering, and finance.

speaker: NORA
text: And size?

speaker: JAMES
text: Revenue and headcount aren't public. The figures we have are the company's own: five hundred and twenty plus customer companies and three hundred and fifty thousand plus learners. Those are cumulative-sounding numbers, so I'd be careful reading them as current active users.

speaker: NORA
text: Good caveat. "Served" isn't the same as "using this month".

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. It's a common way for training companies to describe their reach, and it's not wrong, but it's not a revenue figure either.

speaker: NORA
text: You keep saying role-based. What does that mean in practice?

speaker: JAMES
text: Think about how different the jobs inside a procurement function are. A junior buyer processing purchase orders needs to know systems, policies and basic supplier communication. A category manager responsible for, say, all packaging spend needs market analysis, sourcing strategy and negotiation. A supplier relationship manager needs performance management and risk. A supply chain planner needs forecasting and inventory. A trade compliance specialist needs customs and sanctions knowledge. Role-based means the training is organised around those jobs, rather than around topics.

speaker: NORA
text: So a new category manager gets a path, not a menu.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the idea. And for the employer, it means they can describe what good looks like for each role and see who's on the way there. That's harder to copy than a single course, because it requires a model of the profession, not just content.

speaker: NORA
text: Ownership history.

speaker: JAMES
text: Before Levine Leichtman, the company was owned by Finco, a private equity firm from Antwerp, founded in 1998. That's probably part of the Belgian connection. Levine Leichtman bought the business from Finco in what's called a secondary buyout, meaning one private equity owner selling to another. A transaction database dates it to the fourth of May 2020. Levine Leichtman itself lists the investment as April 2020, made through its European fund. The deal value wasn't disclosed.

speaker: NORA
text: April 2020. Right at the start of the pandemic.

speaker: JAMES
text: Which, for a digital training company, was arguably good timing. In general, that period pushed a lot of corporate training online very quickly.

speaker: NORA
text: And since then?

speaker: JAMES
text: A few things. In December 2023, the company announced new names for its technology, which is when its platform branding, SDX, comes into the picture. In February 2024 it bought Content Enablers, a UK-based trade compliance e-learning company that the announcement says had more than twenty years of history and more than one hundred and fifty cloud-based courses. Terms weren't disclosed.

speaker: NORA
text: Trade compliance. Explain that.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's the set of rules around moving goods across borders. Customs classifications, export controls, sanctions, tariffs, rules of origin. If a company gets it wrong, it can face fines, delays or worse. And it changes constantly, especially in a period of tariff shifts and sanctions.

speaker: NORA
text: So it's a natural extension of procurement.

speaker: JAMES
text: Very natural. The buyer negotiating with an overseas supplier needs to understand the trade compliance consequences of the deal. Putting both under one roof makes sense.

speaker: NORA
text: Anything else?

speaker: JAMES
text: A refinancing. An advisory firm called Clearwater says it helped Skill Dynamics raise new debt facilities to fund further acquisitions. The date and the amount weren't disclosed. But the purpose is clear: more buy-and-build. And Clearwater's description mentions an AI-powered skill assessment tool that builds tailored learning plans, which is an early hint of the AI direction.

speaker: NORA
text: And one odd item, you said?

speaker: JAMES
text: A small one. On the thirtieth of October 2025, the company put out a press release saying it was unaffected by a Microsoft Azure outage. That's interesting mostly for what it signals: customers rely on the platform being up, and the company felt it was worth reassuring them.

speaker: NORA
text: How long has the current owner held it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Since spring 2020, so about six and a half years. That's a mature hold in private equity terms. With a refinancing to fund more acquisitions and a new AI product, the next couple of years look like the period where the company shows what it can become before any sale.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about the customer problem. Why would a company pay for procurement training?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because procurement controls a huge share of a company's spending. In many large businesses, the money spent with suppliers is a big part of total costs. So a skilled buyer who negotiates a slightly better price, spots a risky supplier early, or avoids a compliance mistake can be worth a great deal. That's general background, but it's why procurement leaders care about capability.

speaker: NORA
text: And what makes it hard?

speaker: JAMES
text: Several things. First, the job has changed. Procurement used to be seen mainly as buying at the lowest price. Now it's expected to manage supplier risk, sustainability, resilience, and increasingly to work with AI tools. Skill Dynamics' own blog makes that argument, that procurement is being redefined as strategic. Second, the world has been volatile. Pandemic disruption, shipping problems, tariffs and sanctions all land on the procurement desk.

speaker: NORA
text: And third?

speaker: JAMES
text: People churn. Buyers move between companies, get promoted, or leave the profession. The company's own releases point to churn as a driver. Every time an experienced buyer leaves, the team loses knowledge, and a newer person has to get up to speed.

speaker: NORA
text: So what do companies do today?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general, a mix. Some send people for professional qualifications, like those from the Chartered Institute of Procurement and Supply, known as CIPS, which is a well-known professional body in the field. Some buy general e-learning libraries. Some rely on on-the-job learning from senior colleagues. And some buy specialist programmes like Skill Dynamics'.

speaker: NORA
text: And how do they know it worked?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the weak spot of the whole industry. Most training is measured by completions. Did the person finish the course? Did they pass the quiz? Skill Dynamics' own report argues that this is the wrong measure, and that training should be judged on outcomes. Did negotiations go better? Were compliance errors avoided?

speaker: NORA
text: That's easy to say and hard to measure.

speaker: JAMES
text: Very hard. But if a training company can measure outcomes, it changes the conversation from a cost line in the learning budget to an investment in procurement performance.

speaker: NORA
text: And AI is changing the procurement job itself, isn't it?

speaker: JAMES
text: It is, in general. Procurement software vendors are adding AI that drafts sourcing documents, analyses spend, summarises contracts and flags supplier risk. Some are experimenting with automated negotiation for low-value, routine purchases. So the buyer of the future spends less time on admin and more on judgment, relationships and complex negotiations.

speaker: NORA
text: Which means the skills they need shift.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. They need to know how to use AI tools well, how to check their output, and how to do the human parts of the job better. That's why it's notable that Skill Dynamics' own survey found AI and automation to be the top skills gap. Whatever you think of vendor surveys, that finding fits the direction of the profession.

speaker: NORA
text: So there's a double effect. AI threatens the content business, but it also creates a whole new thing to teach.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the paradox at the heart of this company. AI makes some of what it sells cheaper, and makes some of what customers need more urgent. Teaching procurement teams how to work with AI could be one of its biggest opportunities, and we'll come back to that.

speaker: NORA
text: What does Skill Dynamics actually sell?

speaker: JAMES
text: From the public descriptions, three main layers. First, role-based programmes. Instead of a library of disconnected courses, the idea is that a category manager, a buyer, a supply chain planner or a trade compliance specialist gets a structured path for their role. Second, skills assessment. Learners are assessed against a framework of skills, so the company and the employer can see where the gaps are. Third, the platform, which it calls SDX, that delivers the content and the assessments.

speaker: NORA
text: And how do the pieces fit together?

speaker: JAMES
text: The general logic is: assess, then assign, then learn, then reassess. You assess a team, you see who's strong in negotiation but weak in contract management, for example. You assign learning to fill the gaps. Over time you reassess to show improvement. Clearwater's description of an AI-powered assessment tool that builds tailored learning plans fits that loop.

speaker: NORA
text: And the trade compliance content?

speaker: JAMES
text: That came largely through Content Enablers, with its hundred and fifty plus courses. It adds a topic area where the content goes out of date fast, because rules change. That's both a challenge, because keeping it current costs money, and an opportunity, because customers need someone to keep them current.

speaker: NORA
text: Who's the buyer inside the customer?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general, it's often the chief procurement officer or head of supply chain, sometimes working with the learning and development team. The procurement leader cares about capability and results. The learning team cares about the platform, integration with the company's other systems, and reporting. Selling to both is part of the job.

speaker: NORA
text: Is it sold per learner?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find pricing. In general, corporate training is often sold as an annual subscription based on the number of learners, sometimes with professional services on top for custom programmes. I'd assume something along those lines, but that's an inference.

speaker: NORA
text: And how does it fit into the customer's other systems?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general, big companies have a learning management system, the central place where employees find and record training, plus HR systems that track roles and performance. A specialist provider usually has to connect into those, so that completions and assessments show up in the employer's records. That integration work is unglamorous but important, because the learning team won't buy something that creates a separate island of data.

speaker: NORA
text: And for AI tools, that gets more complicated.

speaker: JAMES
text: It does. A role-play session with an avatar produces a lot more data than a quiz score. Transcripts, feedback, scores on different skills. Deciding what flows back into the employer's systems, and what stays private to the learner, is a design question with real privacy implications.

speaker: NORA
text: How big is the market?

speaker: JAMES
text: For corporate training overall, there are two estimates we found, and they disagree. Grand View Research, in a report published in June 2026, puts the global corporate training market at about four hundred and twenty-seven billion dollars in 2025, growing to about seven hundred and seventy-eight billion by 2033, a compound growth rate of nearly eight percent. Research and Markets, in January 2026, puts it at about four hundred and eighteen billion in 2025, growing to about five hundred and forty-one billion by 2030, at around five percent a year.

speaker: NORA
text: So similar starting points, different growth.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right, so treat the range as wide. And importantly, that's all corporate training: technical, compliance, soft skills, sales and more. We didn't find a reliable size for procurement and supply chain training specifically. Skill Dynamics plays in a small, specialised slice of that big number.

speaker: NORA
text: And competitors?

speaker: JAMES
text: The one we could verify in our sources is Skillsoft, a large enterprise learning company with a broad catalogue. According to a summary of its release, it launched a personalised AI coach on its Percipio platform in early access in August 2026. Skillsoft is horizontal, meaning it covers many topics, not procurement specifically.

speaker: NORA
text: Others?

speaker: JAMES
text: From general knowledge, and we didn't verify these in our sources. CIPS, the professional body, whose qualifications compete for the same development budgets. LinkedIn Learning, owned by Microsoft, a broad low-cost library. Coursera and Udemy Business, big online learning marketplaces. And various trade compliance training specialists, the space Content Enablers came from.

speaker: NORA
text: And then there's the competitor that isn't a company.

speaker: JAMES
text: General AI. That's the one I'd watch most closely. A buyer can now ask a general AI assistant to explain incoterms, draft a negotiation plan or summarise sanctions rules, for free or for the price of a subscription they already have. That doesn't replace structured training, but it does reduce the perceived value of a content library.

speaker: NORA
text: So how does a specialist defend itself?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, three ways. Depth, meaning content and scenarios specific to procurement that general tools don't do well. Measurement, meaning assessments and data that show capability improving. And practice, meaning realistic rehearsal that a general chatbot doesn't offer out of the box. Notice that the AI suite is aimed at the second and third.

speaker: NORA
text: How does a procurement leader actually choose between these options?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general, it often comes down to a few questions. Is it specific to our people's jobs, or generic? Can we see who has improved? Does it connect to our learning systems? Is it recognised, in the way a professional qualification is? And what does it cost per person compared with the library we already pay for?

speaker: NORA
text: And the professional qualification is a tough competitor on recognition.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is. A qualification travels with the person and appears on their CV. A vendor programme mostly lives inside the employer. Specialists tend to position themselves as complementary, focused on applied skills inside the job rather than a credential. That's a reasonable position, but it means the specialist has to prove impact on the job, which brings us right back to outcomes.

speaker: NORA
text: You mentioned a skills report.
chapter: What the company's own research says

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes, the Skills Report 2026, published by Skill Dynamics around April 2026. Vendor-authored, and the page doesn't state the sample size, so please treat the numbers as directional. But they're interesting.
chapter: What the company's own research says

speaker: NORA
text: Go on.
chapter: What the company's own research says

speaker: JAMES
text: Over ninety percent of organisations surveyed reported at least one critical skills gap. The top gap was AI and automation. Sixty percent said they'd been hit by tariffs and trade disruption. And only seven percent said trade compliance expertise was well spread across their teams.
chapter: What the company's own research says

speaker: NORA
text: Seven percent. That's tiny.
chapter: What the company's own research says

speaker: JAMES
text: It is, and if it's anywhere near representative, it says trade compliance knowledge is concentrated in a few people at most companies. Which connects neatly to the Content Enablers acquisition.
chapter: What the company's own research says

speaker: NORA
text: And it says budgets are low?
chapter: What the company's own research says

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes, the report argues that budgets remain low and that training is measured by completions rather than outcomes. Remember, this is a training company saying customers should invest more in training and measure it better. That's not a reason to dismiss it, but it's a reason to read it as a pitch as well as research.
chapter: What the company's own research says

speaker: NORA
text: Fair. Every vendor's survey finds that you need what the vendor sells.
chapter: What the company's own research says

speaker: JAMES
text: Usually, yes. Though I'd say the AI and tariff findings are consistent with what you'd expect from general news. Procurement teams have had a rough few years, and AI is arriving in their tools whether they're ready or not.
chapter: What the company's own research says

speaker: NORA
text: Let's get to the launch. What did they announce?

speaker: JAMES
text: On the eighth of July 2026, Skill Dynamics launched an AI Learning Suite inside its SDX platform. Three tools. Coach is AI avatar role-play, for practising things like supplier negotiations and compliance disputes. Pulse turns material into AI-generated podcast-style audio and PDF insights. And Expert is a chat assistant grounded in the company's own content library.

speaker: NORA
text: Is it available now?

speaker: JAMES
text: The release said wider market availability would come later in 2026, and no pricing was given. So as we record in November, we'd describe it as launched, with general availability expected around now, but we haven't seen confirmation of pricing or broad rollout. It was also covered in the trade press, including SupplyChainBrain.

speaker: NORA
text: Take them one at a time. Coach first.

speaker: JAMES
text: Coach is the most interesting, in my view. The idea is that a learner sits down with an AI avatar playing, say, a supplier's sales director, and practises the negotiation. The avatar pushes back, makes arguments, maybe refuses to move on price. The learner tries different approaches. Afterwards, presumably, they get feedback.

speaker: NORA
text: Like a flight simulator for negotiation.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a good analogy. Pilots don't learn emergencies by reading about them. They practise in a simulator. Negotiators have traditionally practised with role-plays in workshops, which are expensive, infrequent and awkward. An AI role-play partner available any time could make practice far more frequent.

speaker: NORA
text: Pulse?

speaker: JAMES
text: Pulse is about format. Turning content into audio and short summaries, so people can learn on a commute. Useful, but in my view, the least differentiated of the three, because many tools now do that.

speaker: NORA
text: And Expert?

speaker: JAMES
text: Expert is a chat assistant that answers questions using the company's content library. The key word is grounded. Instead of a general chatbot that might invent an answer, it's meant to draw on curated procurement and compliance material. That's valuable if the content is good and the answers point back to sources.

speaker: NORA
text: Is anyone else doing this?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes, and quickly. Skillsoft's AI coach came out in early access within weeks of Skill Dynamics' launch. So AI role-play and coaching is becoming a product category across corporate learning. That's validation that the idea is right, and a warning that it won't stay unique for long.

speaker: NORA
text: Any other public evidence of AI at the company?

speaker: JAMES
text: The Clearwater mention of an AI-powered assessment tool, and the private equity firm describing the company as AI-enhanced. We found no AI acquisitions, no named AI hires and no AI partnerships. And we didn't find a published AI governance or security statement, though we didn't check every trust page.

speaker: NORA
text: Do we know how they built it? In-house, or on someone else's models?

speaker: JAMES
text: We don't. The release doesn't say which underlying AI models or avatar technology are used. In general, companies of this size usually build on large models from the major AI providers and on specialist avatar and voice vendors, and put their own content, scenarios and feedback logic on top. If that's the case here, the differentiation isn't the model. It's the scenarios, the scoring and the procurement expertise behind the feedback.

speaker: NORA
text: Which is fine, as long as they're honest about it.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's not just fine, it's sensible. Building your own large model would be a poor use of money for a training company. But it does mean costs and capabilities depend partly on suppliers, and that's worth managing. A procurement training company, of all businesses, should be good at negotiating with its AI suppliers.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's make Coach concrete. Walk me through it. Invented example.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Let's go back to our buyer from the cold open. Call her Elena. She's a category manager at a mid-sized European manufacturer, responsible for a family of machined components. Her biggest supplier has announced a twelve percent price increase, citing tariffs. She has a call on Thursday.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: What does she do today, without the tool?
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: In a typical company, she reads the supplier's letter, pulls the spend data, maybe asks her manager for advice. She might remember a negotiation module from a course two years ago. She writes some notes. On Thursday she goes in, and the supplier's sales director, who does this every week, sets the pace. Elena concedes eight percent and feels she could have done better, but she isn't sure what she'd have done differently.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And with Coach?
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: On Tuesday, Elena opens Coach and sets up a scenario: supplier price increase, tariff justification, long relationship, alternative suppliers exist but switching is slow. The AI avatar plays the sales director. In the first run, the avatar opens hard: the increase is non-negotiable, everyone's paying it. Elena accepts the framing too quickly and starts negotiating the number down.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And then?
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: At the end, she gets feedback. Something like: you didn't ask what share of the increase is actually tariff-related, you didn't mention the volume commitment you could offer, and you made the first concession. She runs it again. This time she asks for the cost breakdown, separates the tariff element from the rest, and proposes a phased increase linked to a longer contract.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And she can do it a third time.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: As many as she likes. And the trade compliance angle comes in too. Elena asks Expert whether the tariff the supplier is citing actually applies to these components, given their origin. Expert answers from the compliance content and points her to the relevant course module. She realises part of the supplier's justification may not apply.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: So on Thursday she walks in prepared.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Better prepared. She knows the questions to ask and she's practised her responses. Maybe she settles at five percent with a longer contract, rather than eight. In this invented example, that difference on a large spend category could be worth far more than the training costs.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: That's the outcome story.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly, and it's the story Skill Dynamics needs to be able to tell with real customers. Not "Elena completed three modules", but "Elena's team negotiated better outcomes after using Coach". If it can measure that, even roughly, the product sells itself.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Let me push back. Can an avatar really play a tough negotiator?
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Fair challenge. It won't be as good as an experienced human coach. But it's available at eleven at night, never gets tired, and can be set to be difficult. The question is whether it's good enough to make practice useful, and whether the feedback is accurate. That's what customers will judge in the first year.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do a compliance example too. Same company, different person.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. Imagine Elena's colleague, Tomasz, who handles trade compliance for imports. On a Monday morning, news breaks that a new set of sanctions or tariff measures will apply to certain goods from a particular country in thirty days. Tomasz has to work out which of his company's purchases are affected, what documentation changes, and what to tell the buyers.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And today?
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Today he reads the official notices, which are long and technical, checks industry newsletters, maybe calls an external adviser, and builds a spreadsheet. Meanwhile, four buyers email him asking, does this affect my supplier? He's the one person in the company who really knows this area. Remember the company's own survey finding that only seven percent of organisations say trade compliance expertise is well spread.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: He's the bottleneck.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: He's the bottleneck. In the better world, the training provider's compliance content is updated quickly, with AI drafting a summary of the change and experts reviewing it before it's published. A short module goes out to the relevant buyers. And Expert, the assistant, can answer the routine questions, like what does this change mean for goods classified under this heading, with a link to the updated material and a clear note to check with Tomasz for specific decisions.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: So Tomasz handles the hard cases, not the hundredth repeat of the same question.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. That's the value. Not replacing the expert, but spreading the basics so the expert can focus. And I want to stress, for a regulated area like sanctions, the assistant should never be the final word. It's a guide to the material, with a human accountable for decisions.
chapter: A negotiation rehearsal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk challenges.

speaker: JAMES
text: The biggest is the one we started with. General AI reduces willingness to pay for content libraries. If a company's revenue has historically been based on access to content, and content becomes cheap, prices come under pressure. That's our inference, but the chief executive's own framing suggests the company sees it too.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Monetisation of the AI tools. The release positions them as complementary to the core programmes. That's sensible for adoption, but it raises the question of how they're priced. Are they bundled in, which helps retention but adds cost? Or sold as a premium, which adds revenue but needs a clear value story? We don't know yet.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Competition from horizontal platforms. Skillsoft and others can bundle AI coaching into big enterprise deals covering every topic. A procurement leader might get "good enough" negotiation practice as part of a company-wide learning contract. Skill Dynamics has to be clearly better for procurement specifically.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Integration and focus. A buy-and-build strategy, funded by a refinancing, means more acquisitions to integrate, more content to align, and more platform work, all while building new AI products. That stretches a mid-sized team.

speaker: NORA
text: And the cost of running AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a real one, in general. Avatar role-play with voice and video, and chat assistants used heavily, cost money every time they run. Content libraries are cheap to serve once built. AI features have ongoing compute costs. The pricing has to cover that.

speaker: NORA
text: Anything about trust?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. Corporates will ask where their data goes, especially when learners describe real supplier situations to an AI coach. Elena might type in real prices and supplier names. We didn't find public statements on AI governance or security certifications. For enterprise buyers, that's increasingly a requirement, not a nice-to-have.

speaker: NORA
text: And visibility generally?

speaker: JAMES
text: Revenue, margin and growth aren't public, so we can't test the economics. And the headquarters question, small as it is, shows how hard it can be to get a clear picture from outside.

speaker: NORA
text: What about making content in the first place? Has AI changed that?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's changed it a lot across the industry, in general. Drafting scripts, generating quizzes, producing video with synthetic presenters, translating. That lowers the cost of producing content for everyone, including competitors and customers' own learning teams. So a company like Skill Dynamics gets cheaper production, but so does everyone else. The advantage only lasts if its subject experts and scenarios are better.

speaker: NORA
text: So the cost advantage gets competed away.

speaker: JAMES
text: Largely, in my view. The durable advantage is the expertise, the role models of the profession, the assessments and the customer relationships. Not the production cost.

speaker: NORA
text: Okay, opportunities. Where would you push?

speaker: JAMES
text: First, make Coach a product in its own right, for negotiation and compliance practice, priced per seat, and tied to measured outcomes. The company's own argument is that completions are the wrong metric. So build the metric. Track practice sessions, assessment improvements and, with customer permission, negotiation results.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Use Expert internally and externally to cut support costs. Many learner questions are routine: where do I find this, what does this term mean, which course covers that. A grounded assistant can answer them and free up the team for higher-value work.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Use AI to update and localise content faster. Trade compliance rules change with sanctions and tariffs. Keeping a hundred and fifty plus courses current, in several languages, is expensive. AI can draft updates and translations for experts to review. That's a cost saving and a speed advantage.

speaker: NORA
text: And growth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cross-selling trade compliance into procurement accounts, and the reverse. If sixty percent of organisations in the company's survey were hit by tariffs, there's an obvious conversation to have with every procurement customer.

speaker: NORA
text: Acquisitions?

speaker: JAMES
text: The refinancing signals capacity. Natural targets might be skills assessment specialists, or training in adjacent functions like sales negotiation, contract management or supplier risk. But each one adds integration work.

speaker: NORA
text: You said you'd come back to teaching AI itself.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. If the company's own survey is right that AI and automation is the top skills gap, then a programme on AI for procurement is an obvious product. How to use AI in sourcing and spend analysis. How to check AI output. How to negotiate with a supplier who is using AI. How to buy AI software and manage its risks, which is itself a procurement task. That's content general tools can't easily replace, because it's about judgment in a specific profession.

speaker: NORA
text: And it's timely.

speaker: JAMES
text: Very. Every procurement leader is being asked by their chief executive what they're doing about AI. A credible, role-based programme with assessment gives them an answer. And it fits neatly with Coach, because you can practise working with AI tools in realistic scenarios.

speaker: NORA
text: Geography?

speaker: JAMES
text: The customer base is global, but the team appears to be centred on the UK and Europe. The United States and Asia-Pacific could be growth areas, though we don't know current revenue mix.

speaker: NORA
text: And the data?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, an underrated opportunity. Skills assessment across hundreds of companies, aggregated and anonymised with proper consent, could become a benchmark. A chief procurement officer would love to know how their team's skills compare with peers. That's a product, and it's one general AI can't copy, because the data is proprietary.

speaker: NORA
text: If you had to pick one AI bet?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Coach, for supplier negotiation, sold on outcomes. It sells something that content can't: practice. It already exists. It fits the company's core audience perfectly. And it can be measured, which is the key to pricing.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: How would you run the next hundred days?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Days one to thirty: pick five to ten design partner customers with active negotiation programmes and procurement leaders who care about measurement. Agree what success looks like: practice frequency, assessment scores before and after, and a simple, privacy-respecting measure of negotiation outcomes, even if it's self-reported to start with.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Days thirty to sixty?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Deploy Coach to those teams with a handful of high-value scenarios. Tariff-driven price increases, single-source supplier risk, contract renewals. Collect feedback on realism and on the quality of the AI's feedback. Have experienced negotiators review a sample of sessions to check the coaching is sound. And settle the data rules: what learners can type in, where it's stored, how long it's kept.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Sixty to a hundred?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Compare the Coach users with similar teams who didn't use it. Look at assessment scores and any outcome data. Then decide pricing: a premium tier, a per-seat add-on, or an outcome-linked package. At day one hundred, publish an anonymised case study with customer permission. Nothing sells corporate training like a peer saying "this worked for us".
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Who owns it?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: One product leader, with the authority to pull in content, technology and sales. And a customer-facing success lead for the design partners.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: What could go wrong?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Two things. If the AI feedback is generic or wrong, experienced buyers will dismiss it quickly. And if the tool is bundled for free to win renewals without any pricing discipline, it adds cost without adding revenue. The test, in my view, is whether these tools drive renewals and higher prices, or just become a discount in disguise.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Let me do a second quick walk-through, from the customer's side. A procurement director deciding whether to renew.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure, invented again. Call him Martin, chief procurement officer at a consumer goods company with a hundred and twenty buyers. His Skill Dynamics renewal is coming up. His finance director asks: what did we get for this money? Today, Martin can show completion rates and some assessment scores. That's a soft answer.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: And in the better world?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: In the better world, Martin can show that his team's negotiation scores improved after a quarter of Coach practice, that his category managers ran a hundred and fifty practice sessions before major supplier talks, and that, by their own reporting, they achieved better terms on several big contracts. He can also show that the compliance gap identified in the assessment was closed for the team handling imports. That's a renewal conversation about performance, not about a library.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: And what does that do to the price conversation?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: It changes it completely. If the only evidence is completions, the finance director asks for a discount, or suggests switching to a cheaper general library. If the evidence is better negotiation results, the question becomes whether to extend it to more people. In our invented example, Martin might even ask to add the trade compliance programme for his logistics team.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: So the AI tool becomes the reason for the upsell, not the reason for the discount.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the whole game. And it's worth saying, a lot of companies listening will recognise this pattern. Whatever you sell, the renewal conversation is easier when you can show the customer what changed because of you. AI makes that measurement cheaper to collect, if you design for it from the beginning.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a privacy issue with tracking negotiation results?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: There can be. Employees may not like the idea that every practice session is scored and reported to their boss. A sensible design separates private practice, where the learner sees their own feedback, from aggregated team reporting, where the manager sees trends. Getting that balance right affects whether people actually use the tool.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Widen it out. Lessons for other businesses?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four. First, if your product is information, AI is coming for your pricing. The response isn't to deny it. It's to move towards things AI makes more valuable, like practice, assessment, data and outcomes. Skill Dynamics' own chief executive essentially said this.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, launch AI as a complement, then prove it can stand alone. Positioning new tools as supplements reduces risk with existing customers. But at some point, you need to show the AI product earns its own revenue.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, measure outcomes, not activity. Training companies have lived on completion rates for decades. Any business, whether it sells software, services or training, is stronger when it can show the customer's result.

speaker: NORA
text: And fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, speed matters in a new category. Skill Dynamics and Skillsoft launched AI coaching within weeks of each other. When a category forms that quickly, the advantage goes to whoever builds the best proof with customers first, not whoever made the first announcement.

speaker: NORA
text: Any lesson for a small consultancy or training provider listening?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. Your expertise is the asset, not your slides. Use AI to give clients more practice and more personal feedback between sessions. That's something they'll pay for that a free chatbot doesn't provide.

speaker: NORA
text: One more lesson?

speaker: JAMES
text: A fifth one, about the customer you sell to. Know how your buyer evaluates vendors. Skill Dynamics sells to procurement people, who are professionally sceptical and trained to ask for evidence. That's a high bar, but it's also an advantage. If you can satisfy the toughest buyer in the company, your case studies carry weight everywhere else.

speaker: NORA
text: Risks.

speaker: JAMES
text: One, AI disruption to the content business, which we've covered. Two, horizontal platforms bundling AI coaching into big deals. Three, budget pressure. The company's own survey says budgets remain low, and tariff disruption could cut training spend as well as raise the need for it. When margins are squeezed, training is often one of the first lines to be cut.

speaker: NORA
text: Four?

speaker: JAMES
text: Leverage and timing. A refinancing that funds more acquisitions adds debt, and the owner has held the business for about six and a half years. That raises the stakes on execution. If the AI tools don't show traction in the next year or two, the story at a sale is weaker.

speaker: NORA
text: And AI-specific risks?

speaker: JAMES
text: Quality and trust. A coach that gives bad negotiation advice, or an assistant that misstates a sanctions rule, could cause real harm. In compliance, a wrong answer isn't just embarrassing. So grounding, source citation, human review of content, and clear governance matter a lot.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a regulatory angle?

speaker: JAMES
text: Potentially, and I'll keep this general rather than legal. The European Union's AI Act places extra obligations on some AI systems used in education and in employment decisions. Whether a given training or assessment tool falls into those categories depends on how it's used, for example whether assessment results feed decisions about people's jobs. A company selling AI assessment and coaching to European employers needs to understand where its products sit and be ready to explain that to customers.

speaker: NORA
text: And customers will ask.

speaker: JAMES
text: Large customers increasingly do. Procurement teams, ironically, are the people who run supplier due diligence on AI vendors. Skill Dynamics is selling AI to the very function that writes the AI vendor questionnaires. It needs excellent answers.

speaker: NORA
text: What should listeners watch?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three things. First, general availability and pricing of the AI Learning Suite. Second, customer evidence: named case studies or outcome data for Coach. Third, the next acquisition funded by the refinancing, and whether it strengthens the outcome story, like assessment or analytics, or just adds more content.

speaker: NORA
text: And a warning sign?

speaker: JAMES
text: If the AI tools end up bundled for free in every renewal without any change in price or retention. That would suggest they're defending the base rather than growing it.

speaker: NORA
text: Quick-fire round. Short answers.

speaker: JAMES
text: Ready.

speaker: NORA
text: What does Skill Dynamics sell?

speaker: JAMES
text: Procurement, supply chain and trade compliance capability, increasingly through AI practice tools.

speaker: NORA
text: Most valuable asset?

speaker: JAMES
text: Its procurement-specific content and skills assessment data.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest threat?

speaker: JAMES
text: Free general AI making content feel cheap.

speaker: NORA
text: Best AI product?

speaker: JAMES
text: Coach. Negotiation practice is something content can't replace.

speaker: NORA
text: Least differentiated?

speaker: JAMES
text: Pulse. Turning content into audio is useful but widely available.

speaker: NORA
text: Will AI replace procurement training?

speaker: JAMES
text: It will replace some of the reading. It won't replace the need to practise and be assessed.

speaker: NORA
text: One thing a chief procurement officer should do this quarter?

speaker: JAMES
text: Make your buyers rehearse the next big negotiation, with a person or a tool, before they walk in.

speaker: NORA
text: Optimist or pessimist?

speaker: JAMES
text: Optimist, with a condition. The strategy is right. It depends on proving outcomes and pricing the AI properly.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me pull it together. Skill Dynamics started in 2011 as Procurement and Supply Chain Academies, rebranded in 2021, and has been owned by Levine Leichtman since spring 2020, after a secondary buyout from Finco. It's led by chief executive Sam Pemberton, and by its own count has served more than five hundred and twenty customer companies and three hundred and fifty thousand learners. It added trade compliance through Content Enablers in 2024 and refinanced to fund more acquisitions. In July 2026 it launched an AI Learning Suite, Coach, Pulse and Expert, with wider availability planned for later in the year. The core challenge is that general AI makes content cheaper. Our view is that its best bet is Coach for negotiation practice, sold on measurable outcomes, with grounded compliance answers and assessment benchmarks behind it.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's it. And my closing thought is this. When AI makes your product cheaper to copy, the answer is to sell what it can't copy easily. For Skill Dynamics, that's practice, proof and proprietary data. For a lot of businesses, it's something similar.

speaker: NORA
text: Next time on Portfolio Deep Dives, episode twenty-five, we stay in education but move to a very different customer, with Schülerhilfe, the German tutoring network competing with free AI homework help.

speaker: JAMES
text: See you then.
